title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks
trick: Repair a shipped benchmark's broken tasks under a fixed defect rubric, re-score every agent on old and new versions, and sweep the wall-clock cap to 32x to see what repairs and timeouts each moved.
framing_stripped: Called 'benchmark maintenance debt' and 'a continuous-validation workflow for agentic benchmarks'; it is (a) a GitHub-Actions triage bot (/audit runs an LLM over the task files, trial logs and community reports against a four-label rubric; /oracle rebuilds the image and re-runs the reference solution; output is a propose-only diff a maintainer merges) applied once to Terminal-Bench 2.0, shipping 28 of 89 repaired tasks as Terminal-Bench 2.1 (released 2026-05-08 per the Z.ai dataset card); (b) a paired re-score of 19 agent-harness entries on 2.0 and 2.1 at the default budget (Spearman $\rho = 0.958$, up to 3 rank moves, five verifier-repaired tasks carry 62.7% of the absolute pass-rate change on the 28 modified tasks); and (c) a wall-clock sweep to 32x the task timeout on six agent-model pairs plus within-vendor harness swaps, showing a $\sim 20$ pp Codex-vs-Terminus-2 gap on GPT 5.4 is mostly speed under the default cap.
method_equations: Trial statistics (sec. 3): for agent $a$ on task $t$ with $n_{a,t}$ independent trials, $\hat{p}_{a,t}$ is the mean reward (reward is 0 or 1); coverage is 'the unbiased pass@k estimator from Chen et al. 2021', $$\mathrm{pass@}k = 1 - \binom{n - c}{k} \Big/ \binom{n}{k},$$ with $n$ trials and $c$ successes on the task. Version comparison (sec. 6.1): agent accuracy on 2.1 against 2.0 across the 19 entries fits $\mathrm{TB2.1} = 2.1 + 1.04 \cdot \mathrm{TB2.0}$ (percent points), Spearman $\rho = 0.958$ with a task-bootstrap 95% interval $[0.881, 0.979]$. Repair concentration (sec. 6.1, Table 7; the paper gives the number, this formula is the card's reconstruction of it): with $\Delta_t = \hat{p}^{2.1}_t - \hat{p}^{2.0}_t$ the per-task pass-rate change pooled over all agents, $M$ the 28 modified tasks and $F \subset M$ the five tasks repaired at the verifier that moved from at most 15% to over 50%, $$S = \frac{\sum_{t \in F} |\Delta_t|}{\sum_{t \in M} |\Delta_t|} = \frac{305.9}{487.5} = 0.627,$$ which reproduces the paper's 62.7% from Table 7 exactly; the signed total is $\sum_{t \in M} \Delta_t = 377.7$ pp-tasks, i.e. $4.2$ pp of pooled accuracy over 89 tasks, matching the fit's $+4.1$ pp at $\mathrm{TB2.0} = 50$. Resource repair rule (sec. 4): for a task whose oracle or verifier binds on wall-clock, memory or CPU, the budget is raised 'to the factor closest to the original proposal or at least $1.5\times$ the observed requirement of the oracle solution and verifier', i.e. $b' \geq 1.5\, r_{\mathrm{obs}}$ where $r_{\mathrm{obs}}$ is the measured requirement; budgets are otherwise left where the contributor set them. Budget sweep (sec. 6.2): the wall-clock cap is set to $\beta \cdot T_t$ for $\beta$ up to $32$, $T_t$ the task's original timeout, and coverage is plotted against budget; the agent may exit early so $\beta T_t$ is an upper bound on time used. Audit agreement (sec. 4, Table 1): Cohen's $\kappa$ on the binary flag over 89 tasks, $\kappa = 0.80$ for Claude Code (Opus 4.6) vs Codex (GPT-5.4) on the primary category; $\kappa = 0.550$ (gpt-4o-mini vs gpt-4o, 69 agree / 20 disagree), $0.769$ (gpt-4o-mini vs gemini-2.5-flash, 79/10), $0.549$ (gpt-4o vs gemini-2.5-flash, 69/20); per-category one-vs-rest $\kappa = 0.60$ (instruction-verification mismatch), $0.59$ (environment), $0.21$-$0.41$ (drift). Workflow vs shipped release: precision 57.1%, recall 71.4% (sec. 4); on Harbor-Index v0.1, 14 flagged of 34 reviewed, 12 confirmed (86% precision, sec. 7).
load_bearing_assumption: That a maintainer-adjudicated repair restores the task its contributor intended, so a pass-rate change on 2.1 measures a removed defect and not a loosened grader. The paper's own evidence strains it in three places: the audit's accuracy is unmeasured against anything but itself ('Because the workflow contributed to constructing the repair set, these metrics measure retrospective agreement with the release rather than independent defect discovery', sec. 4; 'Agreement measures consistency rather than correctness', sec. 4); the one outside check found misses ('Manual review also identified defects the workflow missed: an incorrect reference answer in Lab-Bench, nondeterministic grading in QCircuitBench, and an HLE instruction admitting two plausible correct answers', sec. 7); and the repair convention for mismatches is to edit the test, not the instruction ('Terminal-Bench 2.1 more often edits the test to accept any correct solution', App. A.3), which is the direction a critic reads as relaxation. A second load-bearing assumption is that a trial that ends in AgentTimeoutError is an agent outcome while a runner, provider or sandbox failure is not: the whitelist drops 'roughly 27% of upstream trials' before any number is computed (App. C.2), and the result that 'over 50% of failed trials ended due to timeout' (sec. 6.2) is a statement about the survivors.
weakest_component: (1) The headline lift is the maximum, not the mean: 'accuracy increased by over 10 percentage points' (abstract) and 'individual scores shift by up to 12 percentage points' (sec. 8) describe one agent, while the fitted line $\mathrm{TB2.1} = 2.1 + 1.04 \cdot \mathrm{TB2.0}$ gives $+4.1$ pp at 50% and the pooled Table 7 change is $4.2$ pp over 89 tasks. (2) No replicate floor under the rank moves: $n_{a,t}$ is never stated (Table 7's percentages are mostly multiples of $1/60$, so about 60 pooled trials per task across 19 entries, about 3 per cell; caffe-cifar-10's 69.2% is not, so the denominator varies), no per-agent interval is given, and 'leaderboard positions move by up to three ranks' is read against no single-version re-run spread (the pipeline's CL-W43-14 question). (3) The budget sweep is six agent-model pairs, five on Terminus-2, chosen for cost ('Owing to cost, this condition is run on a subset of the agents', sec. 3), and the 32x cap is 'an upper bound', so the efficiency-frontier ordering rests on a non-random subset; how API latency, rate limits and concurrency were held fixed across the sweep is unknown (not in text), although wall-clock is the swept axis. (4) The repair set and the audit tool are the same people's: 57.1% precision and 71.4% recall are against a release the tool helped build; the only independent reviewer (the Harbor team) found three misses and two shared-grader bugs touching 13 tasks. (5) One benchmark, one version pair, and that pair is one the field has since left: the Z.ai dataset card (fetched 2026-11-08, update dated 2026-08-18) says 'We also believe Terminal-Bench 2.1 is no longer suitable for measuring the performance of the latest models' and recommends Terminal-Bench 3.0.
regime: Benchmark: Terminal-Bench 2.0 (89 tasks) to 2.1 (28 tasks revised: 16 instruction-verification mismatch, 12 task drift, 8 environment; a task can carry several labels; Table 3 marks per task which of Instr. / Env. / Oracle / Tests / Time / Mem. / CPUs changed; 19 of the 28 are 'hard', 7 'medium', 2 'easy'). Agents: 19 agent-harness entries from 13 models (Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT 5.3 Codex, GPT 5.4, GPT 5.4 mini, GPT 5.5, Gemini Flash 3, Gemini Pro 3.1, Gemma 4 31B, GLM 5.1, Kimi K2.6, Qwen 3.5 9B, Qwen 3.5 27B) on four harnesses (terminus-2 for all, plus claude-code, codex, gemini-cli where native); reasoning effort high or xhigh, temperature 1.0 except Kimi 0.6 (Tables 5-6). Trials: per-cell $n_{a,t}$ not stated; about 60 pooled trials per task by Table 7 granularity. Pass bands: the two weakest entries below 40% on 2.0 and losing accuracy on 2.1; fit intercept 2.1 pp, slope 1.04; per-task pooled rates from 0% to 98.3%. Failure mix at the default budget: 'over 50% of failed trials ended due to timeout, ranging from 68% under claude-code to 18% under gemini-cli'; 11.8% of graded timeouts pass; roughly 27% of upstream trials dropped as infrastructure failures before the decomposition. Budget sweep: wall-clock to 32x the task timeout on six agent-model pairs (five Terminus-2 plus GLM 5.1 on Claude Code); GPT 5.4 harness gap $\sim 20$ pp closes, GPT 5.4 mini gap 30 pp shrinks to 5 pp (abstract). Audit: 89 tasks with Claude Code (Opus 4.6), Codex (GPT-5.4), gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o, gemini-2.5-flash as auditors, web search off for evaluation; pilot on 15 tasks and about 1,500 TB2.0 trials. External: 34 of an 80-task Harbor-Index v0.1 snapshot from 29 source benchmarks. Dates: TB 2.1 released 2026-05-08 (Z.ai card); arXiv v1 2026-11-05, v2 2026-11-09; HTML fetched 2026-11-08. Compute and dollar cost: unknown (not in text). Authors: Buchanan, Zhou, Linderman, Re (Stanford), with the Terminal-Bench team acknowledged.
information_asymmetry: (1) Version-level vs component-level. The paired re-score exists at the version level: every agent on 2.0 and on 2.1 with all 28 repairs bundled. The information about which component moved each task exists in the paper's own Table 3 (per task: Instr. / Env. / Oracle / Tests / Time / Mem. / CPUs changed) and in the public file diff (github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench-2/pull/53), but no arm isolates it: caffe-cifar-10 changed all six components and rose 5.0% to 69.2%, and the paper reads the five big movers as verifier repairs by inspection, not by a content-only or resources-only arm. For the pipeline's CL-W44-11 this settles the vocabulary and the ground truth: 'repaired' is defined by the maintainers' merged diff (Table 3 is a hand-labelled component map of that diff, not a release-note label), which is the file-diff definition the thread adopted (R14/U48), and it shows that on 2.0 to 2.1 the version delta was concentrated (five tasks, 62.7% of the absolute modified-task change), with ten of 28 repaired tasks moving down. What it leaves open is the thread's actual quantity: 2.0 to 2.1 had no uniform bundle change (the untouched 61 tasks are byte-identical across versions, so the untouched-task delta the thread subtracts is zero by construction), whereas 3.0 to 4.0 carries a flat 8-hour timeout and image changes on every task; the hybrid arm (old content under the new uniform bundle) that CL-W44-11 proposes has no counterpart here and is unoccupied. (2) Fixed-budget score vs budget-sweep coverage. At the default cap the score mixes 'can solve' with 'can solve this fast'; the sweep to 32x holds the information that separates them, and the paper reads it only for six pairs and one contrast (Codex vs Terminus-2 on OpenAI models: $\sim 20$ pp at default, mostly recovered at 32x). The sentence the pipeline's thread wrote as an item, 'resource budgets are part of the measurement specification and must be validated alongside the tasks themselves', is now in print (abstract, 2026-11-05), so it is settled as a position and occupied as a phrase; the number it leaves open is the version x budget interaction, which Figure 5 shows qualitatively (GLM 5.1 solves 8 more tasks on 2.1 and overtakes GPT 5.4 whose coverage 'barely changes'; Qwen curves 'nearly unchanged') and never tabulates, and the 4.0 flat timeout is exactly a budget change applied to every task at once. (3) Band dependence stated, not measured. 'The two weakest agents, which fall below 40% on TB 2.0 accuracy, both fall below the fit and lose accuracy on TB 2.1', and 'repairs that make hard tasks solvable matter little to agents that rarely solve them' (sec. 6.1): this is CL-W44-11's band quantifier (20-45% under one harness) said as a reading of two points; the per-cell matrix that would estimate the repair delta as a function of baseline accuracy exists in the authors' trial logs and is reported only as Table 7 pooled over agents. (4) Ordering: for the refuted CL-W44-02 ordering clause the paper is a second instance in the same direction on a different pair: $\rho = 0.958$ $[0.881, 0.979]$ across 19 entries, up to 3 ranks, read by the authors as 'the broad ordering is stable under these repairs'; it does not compute an ordering on repaired versus untouched tasks separately. (5) Agent outcome vs infrastructure outcome. The whitelist that keeps pass / wrong / AgentTimeoutError and drops 'roughly 27% of upstream trials' holds, in the dropped set, the environment-side failure share that the paper's own taxonomy (environment issues, 29% of repaired tasks) is about; the decomposition is computed after the information is discarded. (6) Who holds the data: the per-trial logs for 19 agents x 2 versions x 89 tasks and the sweep traces exist at Stanford / the Terminal-Bench team; the project page 'provides a snapshot of the workflow, prompts, and results' (reproducibility statement) and is the first place to check whether the per-cell matrix is public before any paid re-run under CL-W44-11.
occupies: A published, maintainer-adopted continuous-validation workflow for executable agent benchmarks (evidence agent, rubric-bound auditor with four defect labels, oracle re-run, verifier agent, propose-only diffs via GitHub Actions, five repair iterations), its measured agreement ($\kappa = 0.80$ between Claude Code and Codex on 89 tasks) and retrospective precision/recall (57.1% / 71.4%); the Terminal-Bench 2.1 artifact with a per-task component change map (Table 3) and per-task pooled pass rates on both versions (Table 7); the result that repairing 28 of 89 tasks left the 19-agent ordering at Spearman $\rho = 0.958$ while moving entries up to 12 pp and 3 ranks, with five verifier repairs carrying 62.7% of the absolute change on modified tasks; the 1.5x oracle-slack feasibility floor as the resource repair rule; the finding that over half of failed trials at default budget are timeouts and that a $\sim 20$ pp within-vendor harness gap on GPT 5.4 mostly closes at 32x wall-clock; the sentence that resource budgets are part of the measurement specification; and the Harbor-Index v0.1 transfer (12 of 14 flags confirmed). It does not claim, and leaves open: any decomposition of a version delta into content repair versus uniform recalibration (no hybrid arm; 2.0 to 2.1 had no uniform bundle); the repair delta as a function of an agent's baseline band; the version x budget interaction as a number; per-cell trial counts and a single-version replicate floor under the rank moves; and anything about Terminal-Bench 3.0 to 4.0, the pair the pipeline's CL-W44-02 and CL-W44-11 are about.

neighbors.title: Do ImageNet Classifiers Generalize to ImageNet?
neighbors.trick: Rebuild the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet test sets by the original collection recipe and read rank correlation between old and new scores to ask whether the benchmark measures a stable thing (accuracy drops 3-15% and 11-14%, ordering preserved); this paper says 'We adopt the same protocol, and apply it to a different failure mode: task-side defects in an executable agent benchmark.'

neighbors.title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks
neighbors.trick: Catalogue task-setup and reward-design faults in agentic benchmarks into the Agentic Benchmark Checklist (ABC), which cut CVE-Bench's overestimation by 33%; this paper uses it as the audit rubric's source ('The rubric here follows the ABC guidelines') and narrows it to four action-oriented defect labels tied to repairs.

neighbors.title: LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code
neighbors.trick: Keep a coding benchmark fresh by continuously adding contest problems dated after model cutoffs, so contamination is controlled by time-windowing; this paper calls it 'closest in spirit to continuous validation, but instead we focus on repairing rather than filtering' and borrows its numbered-release discipline for task-side defects.

neighbors.title: Terminal-Bench 2.0 Verified: Instruction & Environment Fix Version (Hugging Face dataset card, fetched 2026-11-08)
neighbors.trick: Patch all 89 TB2.0 images so Claude Code runs (procps, core caps) and rewrite 11 instructions to say what the tests check, lifting Claude Opus 4.5 from 52.4% to 57.9% on environment fixes alone; this paper repairs the same 11 tasks, adopts four of Verified's fixes, and differs by editing tests rather than instructions and adding no harness-specific changes (App. A.3); the card's 2026-08-18 update declares TB 2.1 saturated above 85 and points to Terminal-Bench 3.0.

neighbors.title: Harbor Adapters and Harbor-Index: Infrastructure and a Curated Meta-Dataset for Large-Scale Agentic Evaluation
neighbors.trick: Port more than 80 agentic benchmarks into one adapter format, run 8 models with Terminus-2 and native harnesses across 54 of them, and distil 82 hard tasks from 29 benchmarks through difficulty filtering and an audit-and-fix loop (no configuration above 30%); this paper's section 7 is one round of that audit (34 of an 80-task snapshot, 14 flagged, 12 confirmed) and the misses it reports feed Harbor-Index's later trajectory-level judges.

theme_fit.why: benchmark validity and churn measured directly: a paired re-score across a repair, the ordering's stability, the timeout share of failures, and budget as part of the measurement specification are the lane's sentence; it is the maintainers' own version of the first clause of CL-W44-02 / CL-W44-11 on an earlier version pair
wall-clock budget and sandbox backends (Docker vs Daytona) are named as score-moving levers, but the paper measures their effect on scores, not the cost structure or the serving stack underneath

limitations_as_complaints: My audit tool is graded against a release it helped write, so I cannot tell you how many real defects it finds: 'Against the final TB2.1 release, the workflow reaches 57.1% precision and 71.4% recall. Because the workflow contributed to constructing the repair set, these metrics measure retrospective agreement with the release rather than independent defect discovery' (sec. 4); 'Agreement measures consistency rather than correctness.' (sec. 4); the one outside review found misses: 'Manual review also identified defects the workflow missed: an incorrect reference answer in Lab-Bench, nondeterministic grading in QCircuitBench, and an HLE instruction admitting two plausible correct answers.' (sec. 7).

My version comparison drops a quarter of the trials before it starts and never says how many trials sit under each cell, so the up-to-three-rank moves have no replicate floor: 'However, we note that these filtered infrastructure trials account for roughly 27% of upstream trials.' (App. C.2, the paper writes 27% in math); 'Timed-out trials are still graded on the state the agent left, and 11.8% of graded timeouts pass.' (App. C.2); the per-cell trial count $n_{a,t}$ is defined in sec. 3 and never reported (unknown, not in text).

I have shown that the default time cap is an arbitrary operating point that moves harness gaps by 20 pp, but I have no principled way to set it and I could only afford to sweep it on a few agents: 'Owing to cost, this condition is run on a subset of the agents.' (sec. 3); 'An alternative would be to tune resource budgets per task. However, doing so would require repeated sweeps over any resource and would introduce an additional subjective design choice into the process.' (sec. 4); 'The results here show that a fixed resource budget is an arbitrary operating point and that the choice is not innocuous: it can change efficiency conclusions for individual models.' (sec. 6.2).
